data.title: How Trump and Vance came to Jensen Huang’s rescue
data.description: Seated around the table at the White House, the center of American political power, were the tech industry titans with the ability to dominate daily American life: Mark Zuckerberg. Elon Musk. Dario Amodei. But only one, a source said, was the obvious “power broker” — Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.

data.title: Amazon drone delivering shampoo snags on wire and tumbles onto Michigan man’s garage roof
data.description: When James Brennan was waiting for his shampoo delivery last week, he didn’t realize an Amazon drone would hit a wire and tumble onto the roof of his garage. Brennan, of Huntington Woods, Michigan, near Detroit, said he had not requested a drone delivery and assumed his package would arrive at his doorstep as usual. But on Friday, he received a notification from Amazon telling him to keep an eye out for the unmanned aircraft, so he went outside to take a video. “I just thought it would make amusing, amusing conversation over Thanksgiving or at work or whatever,” Brennan said in an interview. “And I was just going to get a shot of it. I never expected this to happen.” He went to the front yard and heard the unmistakable whirling of a drone as it neared. The rotors kicked up leaves, debris and dust, Brennan said, before the drone set the package down and began its ascent again. Video taken from across the street shows the drone hitting a cable, wobbling and ultimately plopping down on Brennan’s roof. “It swayed a couple of times, and then it swayed over the top of the garage,” Brennan said. “It kind of laid down and died. And as soon as it laid down, the motors shut off, and that was it.” Amazon workers responded to the incident quickly and retrieved the problem drone, but the ordeal did cause neighbors to temporarily lose internet access, he said. In a statement, Amazon spokesperson Jack Stelzner said safety is the company’s “top priority” and that “incidents are extremely rare.” “Anytime a delivery does not go as planned we investigate what happened and use the findings to further improve the service,” he said. A spokesman for the National Transportation Safety Board said officials are gathering information and have not decided whether to launch an investigation. Brennan said the damage to his garage roof was “very minor,” comprising only a few scuffed shingles. He said he and some neighbors also got a $100 Amazon gift card for their troubles. Brennan now hopes Amazon will continue to refine its drone delivery system to prevent future accidents. “Until they develop better technology to spot these these kinds of things, this is going to continue to happen,” he said.

data.title: Congress reacts with anger and skepticism about Jensen Huang reinstatement
data.description: The stock market was thrilled with the announcement that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO of Nvidia, but lawmakers on both sides of the aisle reacted with shock — and said they still expect him to answer questions next week on Capitol Hill. “You gotta be kidding me,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told MS NOW when he learned of Huang’s reinstatement 11 days after he resigned in the wake of revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy. In its announcement, the board said it reached the decision after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.” “No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn asked in a post on X. President Donald Trump told CNBC he’d spoken to the board “directly and indirectly.” “One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? This has been a story for a few weeks. We said no, it’s not a problem.” Lawmakers made clear they still need answers. The Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced that Huang was scheduled to testify publicly on Dec. 3. A spokesperson for the House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on Dec. 1. “There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight,” the spokesperson said in a statement. The speedy reinstatement and assurances of the lack of a security risk came after the Justice and Commerce Departments last week shared details about their investigation of Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company tied to Alice Huang, the suspected spy with whom Huang was allegedly involved. Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is also being investigated over concerns that it — and its subsidiaries — smuggled chips to China. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the administration’s “rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act.” “Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat,” Schumer said in a statement. He added that “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.” Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., pointed to Nvidia’s donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project as a reason to give the board’s decision extra scrutiny. “Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom. Huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him,” he posted on X.

data.title: Virginia and Oregon sue over Grok AI’s creation of child sexual abuse images
data.description: Virginia and Oregon sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX Super Intelligence Corp on Monday, alleging the company profited from a feature in its AI model Grok that produces child sexual abuse material and other nonconsensual sexual images from photographs while failing to put safeguards in place to stop it. Several state attorneys general had announced investigations into Grok over similar claims in recent months, but Virginia and Oregon were the first states to sue. The lawsuits filed in state courts accuse SpaceX of misleading consumers about Grok’s safety and failing to put adequate safeguards in place while promoting its “spicy mode.” That mode allows users to take an existing photograph of a person and generate a sexual or nude image or video, according to the lawsuits. Virginia and Oregon accused SpaceX of violating their respective consumer protection laws. They are seeking damages, penalties and court orders forcing the company to stop violating state law. SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Grok is available to users of X, the social media platform that is a subsidiary of SpaceX. In a statement posted on X on Monday that didn’t directly address the lawsuits, the platform’s safety team said it had taken action to block prompts that could generate this type of imagery and worked with law enforcement to pursue people who use the platform to make it. “The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards,” the company posted. Virginia’s lawsuit cites data from a study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate, which estimated that between December 2025 and January 2026, Grok generated and posted on X millions of sexualized images, including more than 20,000 depicting children. Investigators from the attorney general’s office in Virginia found that Grok’s image moderation was inconsistent, and that the bot would advise users on how to circumvent the moderation measures by avoiding words that triggered it, according to the lawsuit. Beginning in January, Grok told users that its image generation features were only for paying subscribers, which did not stop the images’ creation but allowed the company to profit from them, the lawsuit said. States across the US have filed a growing number of lawsuits against social media and AI companies over harm they say the companies have caused to their residents. In an interview with Reuters ahead of Monday’s filings, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said state attorneys general are acting as a regulatory force in the tech industry, including on artificial intelligence, which has faced relatively little federal regulation so far. “In the absence of federal action, AGs have stepped into the breach,” Jones said. SpaceX is facing more than a dozen lawsuits brought by individuals who say nonconsensual sexual images of them as minors or adults were generated by Grok. In the UK, lawmaker Jess Asato is suing SpaceX ‌after Grok users generated sexualized images of her. The company has denied the claims, arguing that obviously fictitious, AI-generated content cannot breach someone’s right to privacy. In mid-January, xAI said it restricted image editing in Grok and blocked users from generating images of people in revealing clothing “where it’s illegal.” SpaceX acquired xAI in February and rebranded its AI division from xAI to SpaceX Super Intelligence in October. Reuters found in February that, even after new curbs, Grok continued to generate sexualized images of people even when users explicitly warned ⁠that the ​subjects did not consent. The company did not address detailed questions ​from Reuters about Grok’s generation of sexualized material. SpaceX is suing at least two people in the US alleging they misused Grok to create child sexual abuse material.

data.title: Trump says he spoke ‘directly and indirectly’ with Nvidia’s board about reinstating Jensen Huang
data.description: President Donald Trump said he spoke with Nvidia’s board about reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO in an interview on CNBC this morning, where he sought to provide assurances to address the concerns of lawmakers and others about national security. “I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” Trump said Monday. “And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company, because that was, to me, a very important part of our country.” The president’s acknowledgment of his role in Nvidia’s board’s decision marks a highly unusual push by the leader of the free world to influence a decision of a major private company. Nvidia’s reinstatement of Huang at the top of the company sent stocks surging after the market slid last week. Earlier Monday, Nvidia said in its statement that it received assurances about Huang from the U.S. government, though it did not name Trump. “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the board said. Trump said on CNBC that the administration assured the company that Huang, who allegedly had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, did not pose a national security risk. “One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? This has been a story for a few weeks. We said no, it’s not a problem.”

data.title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
data.description: The board of directors of Nvidia announced Monday that Jensen Huang, who resigned from the company on Nov. 12, has been reinstated as its president and chief executive officer. The move is effective immediately, the company said in a statement. “The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” The surprise move sent shares of Nvidia surging by 30%, which in turn put the S&P 500 to open higher by almost 4%. The Nvidia’s board decision came after President Donald Trump on Sunday night wrote on social media: “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” Nvidia said its decision to reinstate Huang came after “input from senior levels of the United States government.” It added that, “based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” In his own statement, Huang said he was “honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution.” Huang has served effectively as the unofficial ambassador for the artificial intelligence boom, the companies backing it and the trillions of dollars being spent in the sector. Huang’s removal from Nvidia came after The New York Times reported that Huang had a close relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies believed was a Chinese spy. The Financial Times followed that report, saying that Huang had an affair with the woman. In a memo to Nvidia’s workforce on Nov. 8, Huang said, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” The New York Times also reported Huang had an extramarital relationship with a senior leader at Nvidia who reported directly to him. After Huang’s removal, the board of the company initiated a search for a new leader, reportedly seeking out Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas. However, Haas earlier Monday announced that he was remaining at Arm, with a contract extension through 2033. Nvidia also set up a new “national security and export control oversight” panel in light of the revelations about Huang. Huang had received an outpouring of support from prominent Silicon Valley tech leaders and investors, many of whom clamored for his return. Brad Gerstner, CEO of Altimeter Capital Management, which has a significant stake in Nvidia, wrote in a letter last week co-authored with Atreides Management managing partner Gavin Baker that Nvidia’s board should keep all options on the table, including potentially asking Huang to return. Bill Ackman, an investor and CEO of Pershing Square, wrote on X last week, “If I were in this board, I would not have rushed to judgment.”

data.title: Stocks set for rebound after AI-driven selloff
data.description: Major U.S. stock benchmarks surged in early trading on Monday, as Wall Street sought a rebound after AI-linked stocks dragged major indexes into correction territory on Friday. Futures that track the S&P 500 rose 2.5%, while future contracts that follow the Nasdaq 100 index soared 3.5%. Dow futures showed that the index was set to rise more than 1,000 points at the opening bell at 9:30 a.m. ET in New York. Those moves would be sharp bounce backs from significant selling seen on Friday, driven largely by AI-linked stocks. The Nasdaq 100, which was already in correction territory on Friday, suffered its worst one-week drop since 2020 and wiped out its gains for this year. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 and Dow fell into correction territory, a 10% drop from their most recent record highs. The S&P 500 has seen little upward momentum recently, having fallen for seven straight days, its longest run of down days since the Covid pandemic began in February 2020, noted Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid. The broad selling started in earnest on Thursday once shares of frontier AI developer Anthropic made their market debut. While the company’s shares posted a 17% jump in its first day, shares closed less than $6 away from its IPO price on Friday. Almost as soon as shares began trading on midday Thursday, investors saw tech stocks, chip companies and major indexes decline sharply. Anthropic shares were higher by 4% in pre-market trading on Monday. “Last week was brutal,” said Ed Yardeni, a widely respected Wall Street watcher and founder of Yardeni Research. He said that he had “expected a pullback” but got more than he bargained for. Yardeni sounded a note of optimism though, writing that he doesn’t think last week’s moves into correction territory will become a “bear market, simply because we don’t see an impending recession.” A bear market is when an index or stock falls 20% from its last record high. Still, Yardeni, one of the most optimistic analysts on Wall Street this year, cut his year-end S&P 500 target for the second time since September. He now sees the benchmark index ending 2026 at 7,500, which would be a gain of more than 8.5% from current levels. As of Friday, the S&P 500 is holding on to a less than 1% gain for the year. Some analysts are warning that even if this is ultimately a correction and doesn’t lead to a more dramatic bear market or worse, “the process may still take time,” as Deutsche Bank’s Reid wrote on Monday morning. “Similar volatility shocks have typically taken 6-8 weeks to subside,” he wrote, adding that “history would argue that further downside and volatility remain plausible before a durable bottom forms.” Also providing headwinds for the market, Nvidia is facing its own troubles after the removal of its CEO, Jensen Huang, who departed the company after admitting that he was unfaithful to his wife. One of the women who Huang allegedly had a relationship with was a Chinese asset, which has thrown the company whose products effectively underpin the entire AI boom into turmoil. Nvidia shares sank almost 23% last week, deepening its losses for the year to 33%. The revelations related to Huang have reportedly sparked an SEC investigation of the company, according to multiple reports. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment, while the SEC declined to comment on Friday regarding the reports. The selling in Nvidia shares have also driven its peers lower. “The fear is that tighter export controls will lower the demand for chips and depress their prices,” said Yardeni of the drop in chip stocks. But in early trading, just like Nvidia, chip stocks also were poised for a major rebound. An ETF that tracks the Philadelphia Semiconductor index rose 6%, while an ETF that follows companies that make computer memory and storage rose 9%. One of the potential candidates to replace Huang at Nvidia took himself out of the running on Monday. Arm Holdings announced early Monday that CEO Rene Haas signed a new contract that runs through 2033. Shares of Arm, one of Nvidia’s largest peers, jumped 10% in pre-market trading. European stocks also traded sharply higher on Monday, with the benchmark stock index in Germany rising 1%, as did the European-wide Stoxx 600 index. Stocks in France and the U.K. were higher by about 0.8%. Major indexes in Asia broadly ended lower as those markets effectively caught up to Friday’s U.S. trading action, however the sharp gains in U.S. futures helped boost Asian indexes off their worst levels overnight. After falling at the end of last week, U.S. Treasury yields also rose early Monday. Treasuries are often seen by investors as a safe haven in times of market turmoil, leading to higher demand and lower yields.

data.title: Advocates urge Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI toys as some are pulled from sale
data.description: A coalition of more than 155 child safety groups and experts urged Amazon and eBay on Monday to stop selling toys with built-in AI chatbots, as Amazon said it had removed some AI toys recently tested by NBC News and a consumer group.

data.title: Delta automation system issue fixed but delays remain ahead of Thanksgiving
data.description: Over 1,000 Delta flights were delayed Sunday after an automated system that calculates an aircraft’s weight malfunctioned during a busy time for travel ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The airline said Sunday morning that its teams were using manual workarounds to get flights off the ground while they sought to restore the automation system that ensures an aircraft isn’t too heavy to fly. Hours later, Delta said that system was once again working, though flights were still not back to normal. The airline said it was helping passengers who needed hotel rooms or meals but hoped to have all the delayed flights in the air by the end of the day. On Sunday morning, the Federal Aviation Administration issued about an hourlong ground stop to some flights into Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, which is Delta’s hub and one of the busiest airports in the world. Complying with the weight and balance limits of an aircraft is critical to flight safety, according to an FAA document, and going above the limit can compromise the structural integrity of the aircraft. The agency said on X that the delays were not related to FAA air traffic systems. Earlier this month, a malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers canceled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days after that, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights. The Delta delays come as Americans have been encountering a growing number of problems with technology that are increasingly disrupting their lives. And the disruptions came just days before the Thanksgiving holiday, the busiest travel season in the United States. As of Sunday evening, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 58%, or about 2,000, of Delta’s flights were delayed; it wasn’t immediately clear how many of those involved flights into or out of the Atlanta airport. FlightAware said that about 58% of flights out of the Atlanta airport were delayed while about 50% of flights destined for the airport were delayed. The vast majority of flights at the Atlanta airport are operated by Delta. Delta said about 70% of the delays and cancellations noted by FlightAware were connected to the automation issue and the rest were because of inclement weather. By mid-afternoon Delta was apologizing for the delays, and said it was rebooking customers and providing meals and hotel rooms where needed, and offering refunds if a flight was canceled. According to FlightAware, 3% of the airline’s flights were canceled.
